sentences.text: Taurovenator is classified as a very large carcharodontosaurid, making it one of the biggest terrestrial carnivores and among the largest known theropod dinosaurs.
Estimates based on comparisons with related species suggest the skull was around 135 cm long.
A distinct feature is a postorbital bone that projected outward like a horn, measuring 3-4 cm in height and 2-3 cm in diameter.
The genus Taurovenator was established by Motta et al. in 2016.
The holotype fossil, a right postorbital, was unearthed by Matias Motta in 2005 from the lower member of the Huincul Formation on Violante Farm in Rio Negro Province, Argentina.
This single bone was formally described as the holotype of Taurovenator violantei in 2016.
Taurovenator is classified in the family Carcharodontosauridae.
Motta et al. (2016) classified it as a derived member of Carcharodontosauridae, closely related to Giganotosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, and Mapusaurus.
Taurovenator lived in the middle Cretaceous, approximately 96 to 91 million years ago, in what is now South America.
Fossils were found in the Huincul Formation, which consists of yellowish and greenish fine-to-medium grain sandstones containing volcanic ash, representing a braided river drainage system.
Fossilized pollen from the formation indicates a diverse plant community including ferns, gymnosperms, and angiosperms.

Some paleontologists have debated whether Taurovenator is synonymous with the genus Mapusaurus. Coria et al. (2019) suggested this because their original distinguishing features were shared, while researcher Mickey Mortimer believed it was synonymous due to insufficient diagnostic material.
However, differences in stratigraphic layers suggest Taurovenator, Meraxes, and Mapusaurus may not have lived at the same time, supporting Taurovenator's validity.
